_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: One may not derive benefit: by rabbinic law.
rashi:a1.2: And one is not liable for misuse: if they derived benefit, they are exempt from the offering for misuse, for since neither it nor its value is sacrificed, its sanctity is gone.
rashi:a1.3: And if before the owner achieved atonement: this refers to both of them; that is, so long as the owner has not achieved atonement, [i.e.] he did not want to achieve atonement with another.
rashi:a1.4: It shall graze until it becomes blemished, etc.: this refers to the one whose year has passed, and not to the one that was lost and found blemished, for that one already stands blemished; it is sold at once, and he brings another with its money.
rashi:a1.5: And it renders a substitute: since its value is fit to be sacrificed, for so we said in the previous chapter (Temurah 20a), that something that grazes until it becomes blemished renders a substitute.
rashi:a2.1: Gemara. What is the reason it does not teach them all together, [but divides them]: that is, why does it teach it in two clauses, and not teach all five sin offerings together, but instead separates the first three from the last two?
rashi:a2.2: The first clause is absolute: they always die, even if the owner has not achieved atonement.
rashi:a3.1: Why do I need to teach it in connection with misuse: for this entire mishna is also taught in connection with misuse, as there is a chapter there [in Me’ila] that begins “The offspring of a sin offering and the substitute of a sin offering,” with the whole mishna.
rashi:a4.1: As though it is standing in a cemetery: that is, wherever it is, one views it as though it stands in a cemetery, where a priest cannot go in after it to slaughter it; and it grazes until it becomes blemished.
rashi:a5.1: We learned: a sin offering whose year has passed, or that was lost and found blemished, etc. A refutation of Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish: for he stated without distinction that it grazes, which implies even if the owner has achieved atonement.
rashi:a6.1: When it teaches “dies,” it is about the one lost and found blemished: and below it asks: if so, with regard to what halakha does it teach the one whose year has passed together with those that die?
rashi:a8.1: Rabba said, this is what it is saying: [the words] “whose year has passed, or that was lost and found blemished” [mean] with a temporary blemish; after the owner achieved atonement, it dies. And even if the owner achieved atonement only afterward [i.e., after it was found], since there are two flaws, it dies. And [this ruling] does not refer to the one whose year has passed at all.
rashi:a8.2: And if before the owner achieved atonement: that is, they did not want to achieve atonement with another, it shall graze, etc. And now one cannot object “but it already stands blemished,” since a consecrated animal is not sold on account of a temporary blemish.
rashi:a9.1: It should have said “he shall watch”: that is, since a temporary blemish has already befallen it, it should have taught “he shall watch,” that is, he shall wait; perhaps this blemish will become permanent.
rashi:a9.2: And furthermore, with regard to what is “whose year has passed” taught: since no ruling at all is stated about it.
rashi:a10.1: Its year passed and it was lost: and it was found unblemished and the owner achieved atonement with another; or it was lost and found blemished, where there are also two flaws, and the owner achieved atonement with another: it dies. Before the owner achieved atonement, [i.e.] they do not want to achieve atonement with another: this one, whose year passed and which was lost and found unblemished, shall graze. And when Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said that even if the owner achieved atonement afterward it grazes, [that is] without a loss, for there is only one flaw.
rashi:a11.1: That the loss is effective for it: it works upon it to bring it to death.
rashi:a11.2: Because it is not fit for its purpose: even before the loss, for “in its first year” is written (Numbers 15:27), and this one’s year has passed; that is a disqualification of the body itself.
rashi:a11.3: Which, if not for the blemish, would be fit, I would say: it is merely a disqualification of deficiency, and since it was found before the atonement of the second, it shall graze, and the loss should not be effective to make it die.
rashi:a12.1: Because it is not fit for sacrifice: as any offering.
rashi:a12.2: One whose year has passed is fit for sacrifice: as other offerings. And all these cases that require two flaws are where it was found before the atonement of the second; but if it was found after the atonement, even if there is no flaw there [other than] the loss, it dies.
rashi:a13.1: And did Rava say so: that where it was disqualified before the loss, the loss is effective to make it die?
rashi:a13.2: But didn’t Rava say: one lost at night is not called lost: if it was lost at night and he set aside another in its place, it is not called lost. And according to Rabbi, who says that even if it is found before atonement it dies, this one does not die: since at night he could not sacrifice it, and it is found the next day, it is not called lost, and it grazes if he achieved atonement with its fellow. And here too, since one whose year has passed is not fit to be sacrificed, the loss should not be effective for it.
rashi:a14.1: Nor for its value: for its value is not fit to be sacrificed at the time of its loss, as there is no offering at night.
rashi:a14.2: It is fit for its value: before it was lost.
rashi:a15.1: We learned: in tractate Yoma (62a), concerning the goats of Yom Kippur: if the one for Azazel died, he brings two from the market and draws lots, and sends one away, and the second shall graze until it becomes blemished.
rashi:a15.2: But an individual’s: in a case like this, it dies.
rashi:a16.1: And Rabbi Yoḥanan said: in tractate Yoma (64a): living animals are rejected. The second of the first pair is rejected forever when its fellow died, and when he achieves atonement, he achieves atonement with the second of the second pair. And the first was rejected when its fellow died, as though its year had passed. And it teaches that the reason it does not die is that it is a communal sin offering; but an individual’s dies, and even though there is no loss at all, it dies because of the rejection of the first, since he achieved atonement with another. Evidently we do not require two flaws, and this is difficult for Rava.
rashi:a18.1: [Rava] could say to you: certainly, where there is rejection and he achieved atonement with another, it dies without any loss, and for Reish Lakish this is certainly difficult. And as for what I answered above, “its year passed and it was lost,” I answered that for Reish Lakish, but I myself do not hold so. And if the case of “lost and found blemished” is difficult for you — why did it specify blemished; let it die because of the loss alone, since he then achieved atonement with another — that is not difficult: the rejected are discrete and the lost are discrete, and although it was lost we require another flaw. So I heard, and no more.
tosafot:a1.1: It shall graze until it becomes blemished: this refers specifically to the one whose year has passed, for if it referred to the one lost and found blemished, it already stands blemished.
tosafot:a9.1: It should have said “he shall watch”: Rashi explains: he shall watch it, perhaps it will become a permanent blemish. But this does not seem right to me, for if so, that is the same as “it shall graze,” which the mishna teaches. Therefore it seems one should explain: he shall watch it, perhaps it will heal and become fit for sacrifice.
tosafot:a12.1: If it had taught it with regard to one whose year has passed, there the loss is not effective, because it is fit for sacrifice [so Tosafot’s heading; the Gemara itself makes this point in its second clause]: and this follows the approach of the Ri, that many flaws bring it to grazing.
tosafot:a13.1: And did Rava say so: that where it was disqualified before the loss, the loss is effective to make it die? But didn’t Rava say: one lost at night is not called lost. And if you say: let it raise an objection from the mishna, which teaches that one lost and found blemished dies, even though there is another flaw together with the loss — one can say: granted, from the mishna it cannot object, for the mishna is different, since it was lost before the other flaw came upon it, and therefore it is not comparable to one lost at night, where the flaw of night came upon it before the loss. But against Rava it objects well, for the flaw of its year having passed came upon it before the loss, and that is why it objects from one lost at night. And it answers: one lost at night is not comparable; it is fit neither for itself nor for its value. Here it is implied, as in the approach of the Ri, that many flaws bring it to grazing and not to death.
tosafot:a18.1: Rava could say to you: Rashi explains: certainly, where there is rejection and he achieved atonement with another, it dies without any loss; and for Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish it is certainly difficult, for when I answered above “its year passed and it was lost,” I answered it for Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish, but I do not hold so; and if “lost and found blemished” is difficult for you, why did it specify blemished, let it die on account of the loss alone since he then achieved atonement with another — that is not difficult: the rejected are discrete and the lost are discrete, and although it was lost we require another flaw. End of his words. But this does not seem right, that the statement of Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish should be left refuted, for it is cited in several places in the Talmud. And furthermore, it is difficult that he has not answered what was asked. Therefore it seems to the Ri to explain: just as it was necessary to answer for the mishna, which requires two [flaws], loss and a blemish, so that you must distinguish and say the rejected are discrete and the lost are discrete, so too we answer for Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish: the rejected are discrete and one whose year has passed is discrete. The rejected are not fit for any sacrifice, while one whose year has passed is fit for sacrifice as other offerings.
gershom:a1.1: One may not derive benefit from it: by rabbinic law.
gershom:a2.1: And one is not liable for misuse of it: by Torah law.
gershom:a3.1: If before the owner achieved atonement: [if] its year has passed, or it was found, and they want to achieve atonement with their value: the one whose year has passed shall graze and be sold, and the one that is blemished is sold at once. And they render a substitute, since they have sanctity of value, and one is liable for misuse of them too.
gershom:a4.1: What is the reason it does not teach: the whole mishna together, all five sin offerings that die together, but divides it and teaches the three separately, that they shall die, and the two separately? Because in the first clause, these first three, it is absolute: whether before atonement or after atonement, they die.
gershom:a5.1: The latter clause is not absolute: for before atonement they graze. And what is the reason it teaches it in Temurah? For it says “and it renders a substitute,” and then it teaches “one is liable for misuse of it” incidentally, since it is dealing with substitution; and since it taught substitution, it taught “one is liable for misuse of it.” And there, in tractate Me’ila, there is a chapter that also begins “The offspring of a sin offering, etc.,” and since there it teaches misuse, there it also taught substitution.
gershom:a6.1: A sin offering whose year has passed: even though it is standing in the Temple courtyard.
gershom:a7.1: One views it as though it stands in a cemetery: just as there a priest cannot go to bring it, so too here it is not fit for sacrifice; rather, it grazes.
gershom:a8.1: [If after the owner achieved atonement, it shall die: this implies that it also refers to the one whose year has passed.]
gershom:a9.1: If so, say the latter clause, etc.: [Reish Lakish could say to you: when it teaches “die,” it refers to one lost and found blemished, and not to one whose year has passed. But if it is blemished, why do I need “it shall graze”? Rather, it says “it shall graze” of the one whose year has passed.] Since this refers to one whose year has passed, “if after the owner achieved atonement it shall die” also refers to one whose year has passed, and this is difficult for Reish Lakish.
gershom:a10.1: Rabba said: teach it thus: [a sin offering] whose year has passed, [or] that was lost and found with a temporary blemish, [or that was lost] and found with a permanent blemish: if after the owner achieved atonement, it shall die, for here there are two flaws, that it was lost and was found blemished; therefore it shall die. And the latter clause is not difficult either, for all of it deals with one [case] (the printed text is garbled here): it shall graze until it becomes blemished with a permanent blemish.
gershom:a11.1: For if so: that it deals with one with a temporary blemish, why does it teach “it shall graze”? It should have taught “he shall watch it until it gets a permanent blemish.” And furthermore, since one whose year has passed does not die if after the owner achieved atonement, unless it was lost and found blemished alone, for what halakha does it teach the one whose year has passed? Another version: And furthermore, when it teaches “die” of one lost and found blemished and not of one whose year has passed, [if so,] why does it teach the one whose year has passed among these of the mishna? Rather, Rava said: so too [it teaches]: one whose year has passed and was lost, and likewise the one that was lost and found blemished: if after the owner achieved atonement, it shall die, because each one has two flaws; and it is not difficult for Reish Lakish. And what it teaches, “if before the owner achieved atonement, it shall graze,” refers to the one whose year has passed alone, and not to the one lost and found blemished.
gershom:a12.1: And did Rava say so: that one whose year has passed and was lost dies on this account, because it was lost? But didn’t Rava say: one lost at night and found in the morning is not called lost, for it is not disqualified by a loss at night, since night is not a time of sacrifice. And likewise, when it was lost after its year had passed, when it was not fit for sacrifice, a loss should not disqualify it.
gershom:a13.1: Rava holds: one lost at night is not comparable; that is why it is not called lost. For that one lost at night is fit neither for sanctity of the body, to be sacrificed itself at night, nor for sanctity of value, to sell it and bring another in its place at night. But one whose year has passed and was lost and found: granted that for sanctity of the body, to be sacrificed itself, it is not fit, since its year has passed; for sanctity of value, to sell it and bring another with its money, it is fit. And since at the time of the loss it was fit for sanctity of value, the loss therefore disqualifies it, and it shall die.
gershom:a14.1: [We learned in tractate Yoma: if one of the goats died before the lots were drawn over them, he brings another and pairs it with it; and if after the lots were drawn, he brings two others and draws lots over them and says: if the one for the Name died, this one on which the lot for the Name came up shall stand in its place; and if the one for Azazel died, etc., up to: and the second shall graze until it becomes blemished, and its money goes to gift offerings, since a communal sin offering does not die. As was said above in the chapter Yesh BaKorbanot.]
gershom:a15.1: And Rabbi Yoḥanan said: there, living animals that were fit, and no disqualification befell them themselves, are rejected from sacrifice; and when he achieves atonement, he achieves atonement with the second of the second pair, neither of which died. And the other, the first, whose fellow died: since its time has passed, as he achieved atonement with another, it is like one whose year has passed. And the reason is that it is communal, so it grazes; but an individual’s dies. And this is difficult for Rava, who said that one whose year has passed and was lost, if it was found before the owner achieved atonement, grazes; but here this [first] one is present, standing before the owner achieved atonement, and the reason is that it is communal; but an individual’s dies. Rava could say to you: the rejected are discrete — that is why it would die if it were an individual’s, for it is entirely rejected from sacrifice; and the lost are discrete, for he does not put them out of his mind, as he thinks they will be found; therefore they graze.
gershom:a16.1: Another version: “Evidently, since if you reject it, etc.” [It is] like the first version; there is nothing between them but a difference of wording.
rashi:b1.1: The matter itself: one lost at night. We assume at first that it was lost only during the night and was found at dawn, so you cannot find it lost at the time of atonement, for at night its fellow is not sacrificed.
rashi:b1.2: Even one lost by day too: that was found before the atonement of its fellow.
rashi:b1.3: For the Rabbis say: in the mishna, [one] lost at the time of designation, that is, while its fellow that he set aside in its place was still set aside and standing, and was not sacrificed before this one was found, grazes; as it teaches: And the Rabbis say: A sin offering dies only if it was found after the owner achieved atonement.
rashi:b2.1: Rather, according to Rabbi: who says it shall die. And Rava teaches us that Rabbi says so only, etc.; [one lost at night] goes to grazing, since even if it were standing before us, he could not sacrifice it at night; it is not lost.
rashi:b3.1: At the time of atonement: it was lost at night and was not found again until he had achieved atonement with another.
rashi:b3.2: The initial loss: the beginning of its being lost.
rashi:b4.1: We have a tradition: lost: [if lost] at the time of atonement, it dies.
rashi:b4.2: And not stolen: and if it was returned to him after the atonement, it grazes and its money goes to gift offerings.
rashi:b5.1: One in his flock: that became intermingled in his flock; even though he sees all of them, since he does not recognize it until after the atonement, it is lost.
rashi:b5.2: And even one: of a sin offering, with one non-sacred animal.
rashi:b6.1: But outside: it went off into the wilderness and became intermingled with other people’s animals, and those others themselves do not recognize it. Even so, since there is someone who sees it, for those others see it, even though they do not recognize it, it is not lost.
rashi:b6.2: And all the more so outside, where he does not see it: at all.
rashi:b6.3: Another version: but in the flock, where he sees it, for he sees all of them, even though he does not recognize it, it is not lost.
rashi:b6.4: Ufeligei [a word in Rashi’s other version of the dilemma, which he takes to mean separating]: that is, he will separate it from them later, when he recognizes it.
rashi:b6.5: That he does not know: that he does not recognize which one it is. Let it stand unresolved. [End of the other version.]
rashi:b8.1: Lost in the cup: lost at the time its fellow’s blood is in the cup: it was lost, and he set aside another and slaughtered it and collected its blood, and while the blood was still in the cup, this one was found.
rashi:b8.2: Didn’t he say lost at the time of designation: that is, if it was found while its fellow was still standing [alive], it dies; all the more so here, where it was already slaughtered, and one could say: whatever stands to be sprinkled is considered sprinkled, and it is like one lost at the time of atonement.
rashi:b9.1: When the Rabbis said lost at the time of designation grazes: even if the owner then achieved atonement with another, that applies where it was found before its fellow’s blood was collected in the cup; but here, etc.
rashi:b11.1: Actually, according to Rabbi: and he does not ask about two animals, but about one animal whose blood he collected in two cups.
rashi:b11.2: And one of them was lost: at the time its fellow was sprinkled.
rashi:b12.1: According to the one who said: in tractate Yoma, in the chapter Hotziu Lo: a cup renders its fellow rejected: [that is, regarding] a sin offering whose blood he collected in four cups and from one of them he placed the four placements, as the law of a sin offering requires, he has made those [others] rejected: its remainder is poured out at the base, and they are poured out into the channel. (For it was rendered fit with the four placements; but here, where one was lost.) You need not ask, for certainly the sin offering is disqualified. For there, where all of them are before us, the offering is fit, even though the three cups are poured into the channel, since it was rendered fit with four placements. But here, where one was lost: since had it been before us it would be rejected, to be poured into the channel, now that it is lost there are two flaws, like a sin offering whose year has passed and was lost, and the offering itself is disqualified.
rashi:b12.2: Remainder: that all of them are poured out at the base. But here, where it was lost, the loss is effective to make it rejected, since he did not sprinkle with it in mind; so it is rejected and lost, and the offering is disqualified.
rashi:b13.1: Or perhaps there is no difference: let it stand unresolved.
rashi:b14.1: Mishna. And afterward the first was found, it shall die: even if it was found unblemished, since the owner has already achieved atonement. For where we require two flaws is where it was found and afterward the owner achieved atonement.
rashi:b15.1: He must take it to the Dead Sea: wherever a sin offering would die, money too goes to the Dead Sea.
rashi:b16.1: From this and from that: they combine them together. Since he brings from both of them, they are not [the money of] a sin offering whose owner achieved atonement with another. But were he to bring from one of them, the other would be rejected, for it would be the money of a sin offering whose owner achieved atonement with another. When he brings from this and from that, there is no sin offering whose owner achieved atonement, and it is like any other surplus of a sin offering, which goes to gift offerings.
rashi:b17.1: It shall be sold, and he brings from this and from that, etc.: but if it was unblemished, it is sacrificed and the money goes to the Dead Sea, since the owner achieved atonement with another. And all these follow Rabbi.
rashi:b20.1: And the money does not go to the Dead Sea: even if he achieved atonement with one of the sums after the lost one was found, since it was found before atonement.
rashi:b21.1: If the second was sacrificed before it was slaughtered: [i.e.,] before the first was slaughtered in the buyer’s house to be eaten as non-sacred meat, it shall die, even though it is non-sacred, for it is a sin offering whose owner achieved atonement.
rashi:b22.1: Gemara. Lost at the time of designation: such as this money, which was found before atonement and goes to the Dead Sea if he could not bring from this and from that.
rashi:b23.1: The reason is “from this and from that”: for one cannot say that the owner achieved atonement with another.
rashi:b23.2: But if he brought: a sin offering from one of the sums, the second goes to the Dead Sea, even though it was found before atonement and was lost only at the time of designation.
rashi:b24.1: This works out well according to Rav Huna, who said: below [on 23a].
tosafot:b1.1: Even one lost by day too, as the Rabbis say: one lost at the time of designation grazes. And if you say: let it say that [Rava’s statement] is needed according to Rabbi Abba, who says below (Temurah 23a): all agree that if he achieved atonement with the one that was not lost, the lost one dies; and [Rava] needed to teach us, according to the Rabbis, that one lost at night, where he achieved atonement with the one not lost, the lost one does not die, whereas one lost by day in such a case dies — one must say that this discussion does not hold like Rabbi Abba. So too there are discussions in the chapter Mi SheHaya Tamei (Pesaḥim 97a) that cannot be established according to Rabbi Abba.
gershom:b1.1: If we say according to the Rabbis: who disagree with Rabbi in the mishna: one who designates a sin offering and it was lost, and he designated another in its place and did not manage, etc.
gershom:b2.1: Now, one lost at the time of designation: by day, which is lost at the time of the second one’s designation and not at the time of atonement, and the Rabbis said of it that it grazes, for it is not called lost so as to die; one lost at night, all the more so.
gershom:b3.1: Rather, according to Rabbi: who disagrees with the Rabbis, he said it; and it is not difficult, for Rabbi says so only, etc.
gershom:b4.1: And if you wish, say: actually, he said it according to the Rabbis.
gershom:b5.1: And here, with what are we dealing: for example, where it was lost at night and was still lost by day, at the time of atonement, and afterward it was found.
gershom:b6.1: And the Rabbis say that one lost at the time of atonement dies only where its initial loss was by day; but here, where the very beginning of its loss was at night, it does not die but grazes.
gershom:b7.1: We have a tradition: that the mishna is speaking of an actual lost [animal], and not one stolen or robbed; for [the rule of] a lost one we know by tradition.
gershom:b8.1: For example, where one sin offering got mixed up within his flock and he does not recognize it, or even one sin offering with one non-sacred animal, and he does not know which is the sin offering.
gershom:b9.1: Or if it [ran off] behind the door, and no one sees it.
gershom:b10.1: But outside: if it ran off outside, where there is someone who sees it.
gershom:b11.1: Or perhaps behind the door, where if the owner of the animal turned his face there he would see it, and even so, so long as he does not see it, it is [considered] lost; and all the more so outside, where he does not see it at all.
gershom:b12.1: Another version: but [if] it got mixed up in the flock, where he sees it but does not recognize it, it is not lost, for we say: perhaps he will remember its marks and take it out of the flock. And [Rabbi Yoḥanan] disagrees with [Rabbi Oshaya].
gershom:b13.1: Lost from him: that he does not recognize it.
gershom:b14.1: And not lost from the shepherd: that the shepherd recognizes it.
gershom:b15.1: [Lost in the cup: it stayed lost until they had already collected its fellow’s blood in the cup, and afterward it was found before the sprinkling. If according to Rabbi, one can say: if of one lost only at the time of its fellow’s designation Rabbi said it dies, one lost in the cup all the more so.]
gershom:b16.1: And if you wish, say: he asks it even according to Rabbi, and he does not ask about the loss of the animal itself; rather, this is what he asks: for example, where he collected its blood in two cups and one of them was lost, and according to the one who said in tractate Yoma, in the chapter Hotziu Lo: [a cup renders its fellow rejected. For so it says there: above, regarding the goat of a prince, it says “And all its blood he shall pour out,” and below, regarding the female goat of an individual, it says “And all its blood he shall pour out.”
gershom:b17.1: From where [is it derived] that a sin offering whose blood he collected in four cups, and he placed [one placement from this and one placement from that], all of them, the others, become remainder and are poured out at the base? The verse states: “And all its blood he shall pour out at the base.” One might think that [even if] he placed [the four placements] from one of them, the others are poured out at the base; the verse states: “And its blood” — of that cup alone — he shall pour out at the base, and the others are poured out into the channel.] And according to the one who says a cup renders its fellow rejected, so that it is not poured out at the base but into the channel, you need not ask, for this one too, when it was lost, since he could not [sprinkle] it, all the more so it is rejected.
gershom:b18.1: When should you ask it? According to the one who said a cup renders its fellow remainder; that is Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon, [who said: from where [is it derived] that even if he placed the four placements from one cup, all of them are poured out at the base? The verse states: “And all its blood he shall pour out.” And as for what is written, “And all its blood he shall pour out,” that serves to exclude the remainder in the animal’s neck, which is poured out into the channel. What is the halakha?] Do we say: when we say a cup renders its fellow remainder, that applies where both are present and neither of them was lost; but if one of them was lost, the loss is effective for it and it is rejected? Or perhaps there is no difference, and even so the other is not disqualified? Let it stand unresolved. And the other version says the same, only it changes the wording.
gershom:b19.1: One who designates a sin offering and it was lost, and he sacrificed another in its place, and afterward the first was found, it shall die: because it is lost at the time of atonement. And likewise one who designates money for his sin offering and it was lost, and he sacrificed another sin offering in its place,
gershom:b20.1: and afterward, after atonement, it was found: it shall go to the Dead Sea, that is, in place of dying.
gershom:b21.1: But one who designates money for his sin offering and it was lost, and he designated other money in its place and did not manage, etc.: he brings a sin offering from this and from that, for both are fit to buy from, since the first was lost only at the time of designation; and the remainder, the surplus of this and of that, goes to gift offerings.
gershom:b22.1: And likewise one who designates money for his sin offering and it was lost, and he designated a sin offering in its place and did not manage to sacrifice it before the money was found, and the sin offering is blemished: it is sold, and its law is like the money above. And likewise there is no difference whether he designated money first and afterward a sin offering that was found blemished, or he designated a sin offering first and afterward money, or he designated a sin offering and afterward a sin offering and both are blemished: since they have sanctity of value, their law is one.
gershom:b23.1: One who designates a sin offering and it was lost, etc.: a dispute of Rabbi and the Rabbis. Rabbi holds that one lost at the time of designation dies, and the Rabbis hold it dies only [if] lost at the time of atonement; and the same is true of money.
gershom:b24.1: One who designates a sin offering, and at the time of slaughter it is found to be blemished: he sells it, and it is non-sacred, and he brings another with its money. Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon says, etc. The reason is explained at the end of our chapter: because disqualified consecrated animals are potent enough to impart their status to their redemption.
gershom:b25.1: The reason is that there is a remainder from this and from that; that is why it goes to gift offerings. But if he brought from these, which were not lost, and nothing of them remained, and did not bring from these, the lost ones, the lost ones go to the Dead Sea, even though it was lost only at the time of designation and not at the time of atonement. This accords with Rabbi, who said one lost at the time of designation dies. The first clause is the Rabbis, and the latter clause is Rabbi.
gershom:b26.1: This works out well according to Rav Huna, who said: below, in this very discussion. [A footnote in the printed edition says: up to here belongs to the previous amud; that is, what follows explains Rav Huna’s statement on 23a.] All concede, both Rabbi and the Rabbis, that when the lost one is found and both stand unblemished, if he drew one of them on his own, that is, he did not consult about which to sacrifice but sacrificed one on his own, the second dies according to all. So too in the latter clause, from which we inferred “but if he brought from this and not from that,” why do [the others] go to the Dead Sea? Because he drew one of these sums of money on his own and sacrificed them; therefore the others go to the Dead Sea according to all. And so both the first clause and the latter clause are established according to the Rabbis.
